title: Andal
hook: Andal tells a friend her dream: a wedding, step by step, with the Lord as the groom

segments.voice: Yesterday, Andal and the white conch: camphor or lotus, and a young woman jealous of a shell. Did some ordinary object remind you of hers? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.

Friend, I had a dream. That's how the song begins, more or less, and what follows is a wedding. Elephants first, a thousand of them, the song says, circling round as the groom comes into town. Then the canopy, the drums, the bride's hand taken, the walk around the fire. Every detail is there, the way you'd tell your closest friend the morning after a dream you can't shake. The dreamer is Andal, and the groom is the Lord. Today, our last day with her: the dream, and the ending tradition gives her.
screen: `FRIEND, I HAD A DREAM.` → `ELEPHANTS, DRUMS, A CANOPY.` → `THE DREAM, AND THE ENDING.`

segments.voice: The song is the sixth in the Nachiyar Tirumoli, and it takes its name from its opening words, Varanam Ayiram, a thousand elephants. Here's the shape of it, in paraphrase. Each verse is one moment of the wedding, and each closes with something like, I dreamed it, friend. The town is decorated. A pavilion goes up, hung with pearls. The groom arrives. The relatives gather; the bride is dressed. He takes her hand. They walk around the sacred fire together. He sets her foot on the grinding stone, one of the steps of the rite. It's a full Tamil wedding, told from the inside, by a bride who hasn't had one. Turn it. In the last two days she refused a mortal husband, and envied a shell. Here, at last, she lets herself have the whole thing, in a dream. Turn it again. Some Sri Vaishnava families sing Varanam Ayiram at their own weddings. A young woman's dream of marrying God becomes the song that blesses ordinary couples. And then the ending, as tradition tells it. Her father, Periyalvar, worries: whom can she marry? Then, the story says, the Lord of the temple at Srirangam lets it be known that he will take her. So her father brings her there, dressed as a bride. She walks into the shrine, toward the reclining image of the Lord, and she isn't seen again. Tradition says she became one with him. The texts are her songs; the ending is the story her community tells. Andal's poems don't describe it. In them, the wedding stays a dream.
screen: `A THOUSAND ELEPHANTS` · `THE WEDDING, STEP BY STEP` · `SUNG AGAIN AT WEDDINGS` · `THE BRIDE WHO WALKED INTO THE SHRINE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a dream told to a friend. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one thing you hope for, quietly, the kind of hope you'd only tell your closest friend. Let it be as detailed as Andal's dream: where you are, who's there, what you hear. Don't argue with it, and don't plan it. Just let it be a picture for a few breaths. Then let the picture go, and rest. If you pray, you can hold that hope in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Andal. Her Varanam Ayiram dreams a wedding to the Lord, step by step; tradition says she walked into the shrine at Srirangam as a bride. Today's word.
Your line: Andal. Today, tell one quiet hope to someone you trust, or write it down, the way she told her dream. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Some Sri Vaishnava families sing Andal's Varanam Ayiram at weddings, and celebrate her marriage to the Lord at her temple in Srivilliputtur and at Srirangam.

what a scholar hears: the dream is her text; the ending is her community's story, and the two together made a wedding song for everyone.

notes: Nachiyar Tirumoli 6: confirm the paraphrased sequence (elephants, the decorated town, pearl-hung pavilion, the groom's arrival, the hand taken, circling the fire, the foot on the ammi/grinding stone) and the refrain 'I dreamed it, friend' (kanav kanden thozhi).
'A thousand elephants' is from the song's opening words (varanam ayiram); confirm.
Practice claim: Varanam Ayiram sung at Sri Vaishnava weddings; the script says 'Sri Vaishnava families sing' without a quantity; confirm or soften to 'some families'.
The Srirangam ending is told as tradition; details (the Lord's command in a dream to Periyalvar, the palanquin, merging into Ranganatha) vary by telling.
howItsDone: confirm the celebration of her marriage at Srivilliputtur and Srirangam (e.g. the Panguni Uttiram wedding festival).
Editor: cut the unsourced gloss of the grinding stone as 'the old sign of a steady marriage'; rewrote the garbled closing line ('They only dreamed it first').
